comparison: Both OpenEval and peer reviewers strongly support the cross-species behavioral comparison (C2, C3, C8-C10, C14-C18, C23, C25, C28-C31). All three peer reviewers affirm this as a key strength, with Reviewer 1 highlighting 'clear similarities in motor strategies' and Reviewer 2 noting 'valuable insights.' OpenEval similarly characterizes the evidence as 'comprehensive' with 'consistent patterns across multiple behavioral metrics.'

Perfect agreement on the qualitative behavioral patterns (C32-C37). Both OpenEval and Reviewer 2 confirm the observation of two distinct behavioral patterns (oscillating vs. drifting). OpenEval notes this is 'primarily descriptive/hypothesis-generating rather than quantitatively validated,' while peer review does not dispute the qualitative observations themselves.

Both support the computational model's specification and ability to reproduce aggregate behavior (C38-C42, C46-C48, C50-C51). Reviewer 2 confirms the model 'can reproduce the different behaviors' and Reviewer 1 notes modeling as a strength. OpenEval characterizes the model as 'well-specified' with 'qualitative and quantitative agreement with empirical data.' Peer review R3 also includes C113, C116, C122 regarding model justification.

Strong agreement on the instructed human validation experiments (C52-C64). Reviewer 2 states authors 'convincingly demonstrate' inference of control objectives from instructed participants. OpenEval describes this as 'strong evidence that the model captures behaviorally relevant differences.' Both affirm the validation approach successfully matched model predictions with 10 overlapping claims.

Perfect agreement on the novel metrics and sensitivity analyses (C65, C67-C73). Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges the sufficiency of RMS position/velocity metrics and the convincing demonstration that alternative explanations (effort cost, noise, delays) were ruled out. OpenEval similarly notes the sensitivity analyses 'strengthen the conclusion by ruling out alternative explanations.'

Both support the single-trial metric and classification approach (C75-C81, C82-C91). Reviewer 2 confirms '~95% accuracy' on simulated data and successful inference for instructed participants. Reviewer 1 notes the 'more strict criteria' as 'good improvement.' OpenEval characterizes the geometric interpretation as 'clear and intuitive' with 'strong statistical validation.' Peer review emphasizes the classification validation more heavily.

Substantial overlap on classifier validation (C82-C91). Both acknowledge the classifier's high performance on simulated data and successful identification of instructed strategies in humans. OpenEval emphasizes this as 'critical step enabling inference in uninstructed subjects,' while peer review confirms the convincing demonstration but reserves judgment on uninstructed applications.

Major disagreement on application to uninstructed subjects (C92-C97, C124-C125). OpenEval rates this as SUPPORTED, calling it 'the culmination of the three-pronged approach' with 'sound logic and rigorous execution.' However, peer review rates this as UNCERTAIN, with the editor stating results 'require further validation.' Reviewer 1 notes 'substantial overlap in behavioural performance' and Reviewer 2 questions whether 'monkeys are switching between control objectives' given 'a lot of trials that fall in-between.' This is the core point of contention.

Both support the CST task design and its advantages (C98-C99, C103-C104). Reviewer 1 calls it 'a very useful behavioural task' and Reviewer 2 notes it is 'of considerable interest' being 'rich enough' yet 'simple enough' for parallel investigation. OpenEval characterizes the CST's advantages as 'supported by the empirical results' with appropriate comparisons to traditional paradigms.

Both support the OFC modeling framework justification (C109-C119, with overlap on C113, C116). OpenEval notes the 'rationale for using OFC is well-supported by extensive literature' and the choice of control variables is 'logical and supported by citations.' Peer review R3 confirms the model leverages OFC and can reproduce behaviors, implicitly accepting the framework choice.

Both acknowledge the prevalence of intermediate trials (C124-C125). OpenEval notes 'acknowledgment that many trials are intermediate is important and supported by data.' Peer review R7 (UNCERTAIN evaluation) raises this as a central concern: 'there are a lot of trials that fall in-between' which 'undermines confidence in the binary classification.' OpenEval views this as honest limitation discussion; peer reviewers see it as undermining the main claims.

Both support the acknowledgment of limitations and scope (C123, C126-C128). OpenEval characterizes this as 'honest discussion' with 'reasonable justification for focusing on extreme cases.' Peer review R10 implicitly accepts the framing, with Reviewer 1 noting 'they've done a great start' and viewing it positively as a starting point for future neural studies.

Both support the perturbation paradigm as future direction (C129-C130). Reviewer 1 explicitly welcomes this: 'I'm glad to see the addition of the model performance on perturbation trials' showing 'much greater separation' and states 'I think it is essential for this group to develop the perturbation paradigm.' OpenEval notes this is 'supported by preliminary simulations' and represents 'appropriate suggestions for future work.'

OpenEval evaluates the summary of contributions and neural implications (C131-C135) as SUPPORTED, noting the summary is 'accurate based on presented results' and speculation is 'appropriately tentative.' No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these summary claims.

OpenEval evaluates methodological details (C136-C167) as SUPPORTED, noting methods are 'generally well-specified and appropriate' with 'adequate sample sizes' and 'sufficiently detailed for replication,' though some parameter details could be more explicit. No corresponding peer review evaluation systematically addresses these methodological claims.
